note:
Doctor: Thanks for coming in. Your chart says you're a 32-year-old male here about facial redness. How long has this been going on?
Patient: About eight months. My cheeks and nose get red and flushed, mostly after I drink wine or eat spicy food. Lately I've been getting little red bumps too.
Doctor: Any itching, blistering, or eye irritation?
Patient: No itching and no blistering. My eyes feel fine, no burning or grittiness.
Doctor: Do you have any drug allergies?
Patient: Yes, I'm allergic to sulfa drugs. I got hives from a sulfa antibiotic when I was a teenager.
Doctor: Okay, I'll make sure that is flagged in your chart. What have you tried so far?
Patient: Just a drugstore moisturizer. I take cetirizine 10 mg once daily for hay fever, nothing else.
Doctor: On exam you have redness across both cheeks and the nose, with scattered small red papules and a few visible fine blood vessels. I don't see any pustules, and there is no thickening of the skin on your nose. Your eyelids look normal. This is rosacea with inflammatory papules. Because of your sulfa allergy, I will avoid any sulfa-based washes or creams. I'm starting metronidazole 0.75% gel, applied to the affected areas twice daily. Please use a gentle cleanser, wear SPF 30 sunscreen every day, and keep track of triggers like alcohol and spicy food.
Patient: That sounds good.
Doctor: Let's see you back in eight weeks to check your response. If it isn't improving, we can talk about other options.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 32-year-old male presented to dermatology with eight months of facial redness, flushing, and small red bumps triggered by wine and spicy food, and he denied itching, blistering, and eye burning. He has a documented sulfa allergy causing hives and takes cetirizine for hay fever. Examination showed redness of the cheeks and nose with red papules and fine visible blood vessels, without pustules or thickening of the nasal skin. The clinician diagnosed rosacea and started metronidazole 0.75% gel twice daily while avoiding sulfa-based products. Sunscreen, trigger tracking, and follow-up in eight weeks were advised.

note:
Telephone visit, audio only. The patient was at home and gave verbal consent for a telehealth visit. No video was available, so no visual examination was performed.

Reason for visit: follow-up of generalized anxiety disorder in a 32-year-old male.

History per patient: He works rotating shifts as a warehouse supervisor, alternating between night weeks and day weeks, and says his schedule changes with little notice. He reports persistent excessive worry about work performance and money, restlessness, muscle tension in the neck and shoulders, difficulty concentrating, and irritability on most days. His worry is worst during the first few days after switching from nights to days. He sleeps only 4 to 5 hours on workdays and describes his sleep as broken. GAD-7 was administered verbally today and the score was 15, compared with 12 at the last visit. He denies suicidal ideation, thoughts of self-harm, panic attacks, and hallucinations. He denies any decreased need for sleep.

Medications and adherence: The patient first said he takes sertraline 100 mg once daily when he takes it. On further questioning, and after he read the label on the bottle, he corrected this and said the tablets are 50 mg, prescribed once daily, and that he takes one on only about four days a week because the monthly cost is hard for him to afford since his insurance deductible reset. He also has hydroxyzine 25 mg as needed for anxiety, which he uses before shifts, but he finds it makes him drowsy at work around forklifts. Other medications are omeprazole 20 mg once daily for GERD, lisinopril 10 mg once daily for hypertension, and over-the-counter melatonin 3 mg at bedtime. He drinks about three energy drinks per shift.

Data: Labs reviewed from his primary care physician last month showed TSH 1.9 mIU/L, hemoglobin 14.8 g/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and fasting glucose 94 mg/dL. Home blood pressure today was 134/86 with a heart rate of 82. By voice, his speech was normal in rate and volume, his thought process was linear, and he was cooperative and engaged.

Impression: Generalized anxiety disorder, moderate, with only a partial response because of intermittent sertraline use driven by cost. Shift work sleep disorder is contributing to his anxiety. GERD and hypertension are stable by his report.

Management: Increase sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg once daily, prescribed as a single generic 100 mg tablet with a 90-day supply through a low-cost pharmacy discount program so that he can take it every day. Discontinue hydroxyzine 25 mg because of daytime drowsiness and the safety concern at work. Continue omeprazole 20 mg once daily, lisinopril 10 mg once daily, and melatonin 3 mg at bedtime, timed to the start of his main sleep period. Refer to the clinic social worker for help with prescription cost assistance. Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy by video with evening appointment times. Advise limiting energy drinks, avoiding caffeine in the last six hours of a shift, and keeping a consistent sleep window after night shifts. Repeat the GAD-7 at the next visit. Follow-up telephone visit in 4 weeks, sooner if symptoms worsen. I reviewed the 988 crisis line and when to seek emergency care.

He had been taking sertraline on only about four days a week because of cost, and he corrected his first report of the dose from 100 mg to 50 mg. He denied suicidal ideation and panic attacks. The clinician increased sertraline to 100 mg once daily with a low-cost 90-day supply, stopped hydroxyzine for daytime drowsiness, and continued omeprazole, lisinopril, and melatonin. Social work and cognitive behavioral therapy referrals were made, with telephone follow-up in 4 weeks.

note: This is a dictation for a new patient visit in the urology outpatient clinic. The patient is a 52-year-old male referred by his primary care physician for an elevated PSA. His screening PSA last month was 5.2, correction, 5.4 ng/mL, up from 3.1 ng/mL two years ago. He has no urinary complaints. He denies hematuria, dysuria, weakness in the urinary stream, and nocturia, and he denies any bone pain or unintentional weight loss. No fever and no recent urinary tract infection. He has not had a catheter or any prostate procedure. No family history of prostate cancer. Past medical history is hypertension, treated with lisinopril 10 mg once daily. He is allergic to ciprofloxacin, which caused hives. Vitals today, blood pressure 126/78, heart rate 70. Abdomen is soft and nontender with no suprapubic fullness. On digital rectal exam the prostate is smooth, symmetric, nontender, about 30 grams, with no nodules. My impression is an elevated PSA with a normal rectal exam and no signs of infection. Plan is to repeat the PSA with a free PSA in six weeks and to order a multiparametric MRI of the prostate. I will discuss a biopsy only if the repeat PSA stays elevated or the MRI shows a suspicious lesion, and I have flagged his chart so that he does not receive a fluoroquinolone antibiotic for biopsy prophylaxis. He will return in eight weeks to review the results. End of dictation.

note: Dictating a follow-up visit in the pulmonary clinic for a 29-year-old male with an incidental pulmonary nodule. The nodule was found twelve months ago on a CT of the chest obtained to evaluate rib pain after a fall from his bicycle. It was a solid nodule measuring 5 mm in the right lower lobe. He is a lifelong never smoker with no occupational dust exposure, no history of cancer, and no family history of lung cancer. Today he denies cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. His only medical problem is seasonal allergic rhinitis, and he takes cetirizine 10 mg once daily during pollen season. Vitals, blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 66, respiratory rate 14, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally, there is no clubbing, and there is no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. A follow-up CT of the chest without contrast was done last week and shows the right lower lobe nodule is stable at 5 mm, unchanged in size and density, with no new nodules and no enlarged lymph nodes. My impression is a stable 5 mm solid pulmonary nodule in a low-risk patient, most consistent with a benign process. Per Fleischner Society guidance no further imaging is needed. I reviewed the images with the patient and he understands. He should call if he develops a new cough, coughs up blood, or loses weight without trying. He is discharged from the pulmonary clinic to the care of his primary care physician, and he will continue cetirizine.
summary: A 29-year-old male returned to the pulmonary clinic for follow-up of a 5 mm solid right lower lobe nodule found incidentally on a CT of the chest a year ago. He is a never smoker with no cancer history and denied cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Vital signs were normal and the lungs were clear. A repeat CT of the chest showed the nodule stable at 5 mm with no new nodules. The impression was a stable nodule in a low-risk patient, most consistent with a benign process, so no further imaging is needed and he is discharged to his primary care physician.

note:
The patient is a 77-year-old male seen in the urology clinic for evaluation of a rising PSA. He was referred by his primary care physician after a screening PSA of 6.1 ng/mL, compared with 4.4 ng/mL one year ago. His only urinary symptom is long-standing mild nocturia twice per night. He denies gross hematuria, dysuria, fever, back pain, bone pain, and unintentional weight loss. He has had no urinary retention, recent urinary tract infection, or instrumentation.

His history includes BPH, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, stable coronary artery disease with a coronary stent placed several years ago, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. His daughter came with him and brought all of his pill bottles. Prescription medications are finasteride 5 mg once daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg once daily, atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime, and aspirin 81 mg once daily. His primary care physician increased the lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg two weeks ago because of elevated home blood pressure readings. The patient initially told me he had started finasteride only a few weeks ago, but after reviewing the pharmacy labels with his daughter he clarified that he has taken it every day for about three years. This matters because finasteride lowers the PSA by roughly half, so his measured PSA of 6.1 ng/mL corresponds to an adjusted value of about 12 ng/mL.

He also uses several over-the-counter supplements to support prostate health: saw palmetto 320 mg, which he first said he takes twice daily but then corrected, after reading the bottle, to once daily; fish oil 1000 mg twice daily; and zinc 30 mg once daily. I explained that saw palmetto has not been shown to reduce prostate cancer risk and that fish oil adds to the bleeding tendency of aspirin around the time of a biopsy.

On examination, blood pressure is 148/82 and heart rate is 72. The abdomen is soft without suprapubic tenderness. On digital rectal examination the prostate is enlarged to about 50 grams, smooth, and nontender, with no discrete nodule. Laboratory results today include a repeat PSA of 6.3 ng/mL with a free PSA of 12%, hemoglobin A1c 7.2%, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, and eGFR 49. Urinalysis showed no blood, nitrite, or leukocyte esterase. A multiparametric MRI of the prostate obtained two weeks ago showed a 1.2 cm PI-RADS 4 lesion in the right posterior peripheral zone, with a total prostate volume of 52 mL.

My impression is an elevated PSA, about 12.6 ng/mL after adjustment for finasteride, with a PI-RADS 4 lesion that is suspicious for clinically significant prostate cancer. He also has BPH, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, stable coronary artery disease, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a.

We discussed MRI-targeted transperineal prostate biopsy with systematic sampling, including the risks of bleeding, infection, and urinary retention, and he wishes to proceed. I advised him to stop the saw palmetto and the fish oil now. I will contact his cardiologist to confirm whether aspirin 81 mg can be held for seven days before the biopsy. He will continue finasteride 5 mg once daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily, lisinopril 20 mg once daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime. Metformin 500 mg will be held on the morning of the biopsy. I will see him two weeks after the biopsy to review the pathology.
summary: A 77-year-old male was seen in urology for a rising PSA of 6.1 ng/mL, which is about 12 ng/mL after adjusting for the finasteride he has taken daily for about three years. He clarified his finasteride history and his saw palmetto dose, and he also takes fish oil and zinc. The prostate was enlarged and smooth without nodules, and MRI showed a 1.2 cm PI-RADS 4 lesion. The impression was an elevated PSA with a suspicious lesion, alongside BPH, diabetes, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and stage 3a kidney disease. The plan is an MRI-targeted transperineal biopsy, stopping saw palmetto and fish oil, checking with cardiology about holding aspirin, and a visit two weeks after the biopsy.

note:
The patient is a 71-year-old female with stable exertional angina who returns to the cardiology clinic for follow-up. She reports substernal chest pressure when walking uphill or climbing more than one flight of stairs, lasting three to five minutes and relieved by rest. Over the past month the episodes have increased from about once a week to three or four times a week at the same level of exertion. She reports no rest pain and no pain that wakes her from sleep. She denies palpitations, syncope, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and leg swelling.

Her history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. She is allergic to aspirin, which causes hives and wheezing, and she has never taken it. For that reason she uses clopidogrel 75 mg once daily as her antiplatelet agent. During medication reconciliation she first said that she takes metoprolol succinate 25 mg, but after checking her pill bottle she corrected this and confirmed that it is 50 mg once daily. Her other medications are atorvastatin 40 mg once daily, lisinopril 20 mg once daily, and metformin 500 mg twice daily. She stopped amlodipine 10 mg once daily on her own two weeks ago because of ankle swelling, and the swelling has since resolved.

On examination, blood pressure is 142/84, heart rate is 76, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Heart sounds are regular with no murmur or S3, the lungs are clear, there are no carotid bruits, and there is no peripheral edema. Today's electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 76 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T wave changes, unchanged from the prior tracing. An exercise stress echocardiogram last month showed mild reversible ischemia in the anterior wall at 5 METs with an ejection fraction of 55%. Laboratory results include LDL cholesterol 98 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c 7.4%, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, eGFR 58, and potassium 4.4 mEq/L.

My impression is stable exertional angina with increasing frequency but without rest pain or features of unstable angina, in a patient with hypertension above goal, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia with LDL above goal, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. Because of her aspirin allergy, clopidogrel will remain her antiplatelet therapy and she should avoid all NSAIDs.

We increased metoprolol succinate from 50 mg to 100 mg once daily and started isosorbide mononitrate extended-release 30 mg every morning. She was prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg as needed for chest pain and was taught to sit down, take one tablet, and call emergency services if the pain persists five minutes after the first dose. Atorvastatin will be increased to 80 mg once daily, with a repeat lipid panel in eight weeks. She will remain off amlodipine and will continue lisinopril 20 mg once daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and clopidogrel 75 mg once daily. I referred her to cardiac rehabilitation. If angina does not improve on this regimen or if rest pain develops, we will proceed to coronary angiography. I will see her again in four weeks.
summary: A 71-year-old female with stable exertional angina returned to cardiology because episodes of substernal chest pressure increased to three or four times a week. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and stage 3a kidney disease, and she is allergic to aspirin, so she takes clopidogrel. She corrected her metoprolol dose from 25 mg to 50 mg and had stopped amlodipine for ankle swelling. Blood pressure was 142/84, and a stress echocardiogram showed mild reversible anterior ischemia. The clinician increased metoprolol succinate to 100 mg, started isosorbide mononitrate and sublingual nitroglycerin, and raised atorvastatin to 80 mg, with cardiac rehabilitation and follow-up in four weeks.

note:
Telephone visit, audio only. The patient was at home and gave verbal consent to a telehealth visit. No video was available, so no physical examination could be performed.

Reason for visit: follow-up of left leg pain in a 70-year-old female with lumbar radiculopathy.

History per patient: She reports five weeks of low back pain with burning pain that travels down the left buttock, the outer thigh, and the calf to the top of the foot. The pain is 7 out of 10 at its worst, is worse with sitting and with coughing, and is a little better when she walks. She also has numbness and tingling over the top of the left foot. She denies bowel or bladder incontinence, saddle numbness, fever, progressive leg weakness, and recent falls. She says she can walk around her house and stand up from a chair without help.

Her other problems are hypertension and GERD. Medications she reports taking are amlodipine 5 mg once daily, omeprazole 20 mg once daily, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily, which she has used for three weeks with little relief and which upsets her stomach, and acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed.

Home readings today were blood pressure 138/80 and pulse 72 on her own cuff.

Data: An MRI of the lumbar spine two weeks ago, with the report read to the patient, shows a left paracentral disc extrusion at L4-L5 compressing the traversing left L5 nerve root, with moderate foraminal narrowing.

Impression: Left L5 lumbar radiculopathy due to an L4-L5 disc extrusion, with no red flag symptoms reported. Hypertension is stable by home readings, and GERD is stable on omeprazole.

Recommendations: Stop ibuprofen because of her stomach upset and blood pressure. Continue acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed, not to exceed 3 grams per day. Start gabapentin 100 mg at bedtime, then increase to 100 mg three times daily after three days if she tolerates it, with counseling about drowsiness, dizziness, and fall precautions. Refer to physical therapy for core stabilization and nerve glide exercises. Encourage short walks and avoid prolonged bed rest. If the pain is not improved in four weeks, we will discuss an epidural steroid injection. She was told to go to the emergency department right away for new bowel or bladder incontinence, numbness in the saddle area, or worsening leg weakness. Follow-up telephone visit in four weeks.
summary: A 70-year-old female with lumbar radiculopathy was seen by telephone for five weeks of low back pain with burning pain down the left leg and numbness and tingling over the top of the left foot. She denied bowel or bladder incontinence, saddle numbness, fever, and progressive leg weakness. An MRI of the lumbar spine showed a left L4-L5 disc extrusion compressing the left L5 nerve root. The impression was left L5 radiculopathy without red flag symptoms. Ibuprofen was stopped, gabapentin 100 mg at bedtime was started with titration, acetaminophen was continued, and physical therapy and follow-up in four weeks were arranged.

Doctor: Come on in. Your chart says you're a 56-year-old female here for headaches with visual changes. Tell me about them.
Patient: They've been getting worse over the past year. First I see zigzag shimmering lights on the left side of my vision for about twenty minutes. Then I get a throbbing headache on one side, with nausea, and I can't stand bright lights. It lasts most of the day. I get about six of them a month now.
Doctor: Any weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking with these?
Patient: No weakness, no numbness, and no trouble speaking. I never pass out either.
Doctor: Any fever, stiff neck, or a sudden headache that is the worst of your life?
Patient: No, nothing like that. They always feel the same.
Doctor: What do you take for them?
Patient: Sumatriptan 50 mg when I notice the lights, and ibuprofen 600 mg on other days when it hurts. I'd say I take something about ten days a month. I also take lisinopril 10 mg every morning for high blood pressure.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure today is 138/82 and your pulse is 74. Your neurological exam is normal: cranial nerves are intact, strength is full in all four limbs, reflexes are symmetric, your gait is steady, and I see no swelling of the optic nerves on the eye exam. The MRI of your brain from two months ago was normal. This is migraine with aura. Since you're having about six attacks a month, I'd like to start a preventive medicine. I'm starting topiramate 25 mg at bedtime for two weeks, then 25 mg twice a day. It can cause tingling in the hands and feeling foggy or tired. Keep taking sumatriptan 50 mg at the first sign of the aura. You can repeat it once after two hours, and don't take more than 200 mg in a day. I'd also like you to limit the ibuprofen to no more than two days a week so it doesn't cause rebound headaches. Please keep a headache diary.
Patient: That makes sense. Will the topiramate interact with my blood pressure pill?
Doctor: No, they are fine together. Let's see you back in eight weeks.
Patient: Thank you.
summary: A 56-year-old female with migraine with aura reported worsening attacks of zigzag shimmering lights followed by a throbbing one-sided headache with nausea, about six times a month. She denied weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, fever, and stiff neck. Blood pressure was 138/82, the neurological and eye exams were normal, and a prior MRI of the brain was normal. The clinician diagnosed migraine with aura, started topiramate 25 mg at bedtime to increase to twice daily, continued sumatriptan, and limited ibuprofen to two days a week. A headache diary and follow-up in eight weeks were advised.

note:
Doctor: Hi there. Your chart says he's an 8-year-old male referred for repeated throat infections and a failed school vision screening. Mom, tell me what's been happening.
Family member: He's had tonsillitis seven times in the past year. Each time it's a high fever, a terrible sore throat, and he won't eat, and he misses about three days of school. He finished a ten-day course of antibiotics a month ago, and now the sore throat is back for two days with a fever. He snores at night, but I haven't seen him stop breathing.
Doctor: Any ear pain, drooling, or trouble breathing?
Family member: No ear pain and no drooling, and he breathes fine.
Doctor: And what about his eyes?
Family member: His school said he failed the vision check. He squints at the board and holds books close to his face. No eye pain, no redness, and no double vision.
Doctor: Okay, let me take a look. His temperature is 100.4 F, his heart rate is 98, and he weighs 26 kilograms. His tonsils are large with white exudate, and the lymph nodes under his jaw are tender. His uvula is midline, there is no swelling beside the tonsils, and his ears look normal. The rapid strep test is positive. On the eye chart, his right eye reads 20/50 and his left eye reads 20/40, which improves to 20/25 with the pinhole. His eyes are straight, his pupils react normally, and the front of both eyes looks healthy.
Doctor: So he has strep throat on top of recurrent tonsillitis. I'm starting amoxicillin 500 mg twice daily for ten days, and he can have acetaminophen 325 mg every six hours as needed for the pain and fever. Because he has had seven infections in one year, I'm referring him to our surgeon to talk about a tonsillectomy. As for his vision, it looks like nearsightedness. We'll arrange a cycloplegic refraction with the eye team here so he can get glasses.
Family member: That sounds good. Should he stay home from school?
Doctor: Yes, until he has been on the antibiotic for 24 hours and has no fever. Let's see you back in four to six weeks.

He had a two-day sore throat with fever, and his mother denied ear pain, drooling, eye pain, redness, and double vision. He had large tonsils with white exudate and a positive rapid strep test, and his visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left, improving with pinhole. The clinician diagnosed strep throat on top of recurrent tonsillitis and probable nearsightedness. Amoxicillin and acetaminophen were prescribed, with referral for tonsillectomy evaluation and a cycloplegic refraction for glasses.

The patient is a 20-year-old male with post-traumatic stress disorder following a serious motor vehicle collision about one year ago, seen in the psychiatry outpatient clinic for follow-up. He reports nightmares about three times a week, intrusive memories of the crash, and hypervigilance when riding in cars. He avoids driving on highways. He denies suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation, and hallucinations. He started sertraline 50 mg once daily at the last visit and has taken it every day without side effects. His PCL-5 score today is 44, down from 52 at the last visit.

He lives about 40 miles from the clinic, does not own a car, and depends on a bus line with an unreliable schedule. He has missed two earlier appointments because he had no ride. On mental status examination he is well groomed and cooperative, with an anxious mood, a constricted affect, a linear thought process, no evidence of psychosis, and good insight.

My impression is post-traumatic stress disorder with a partial response to sertraline, complicated by transportation barriers that make follow-up difficult. I am increasing sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg once daily and starting prazosin 1 mg at bedtime for nightmares. I referred him for trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy delivered by video so that he does not have to travel. Our clinic social worker will arrange transportation vouchers for any in-person visits. His next follow-up will be a video visit in four weeks.

note:
Hospital medicine progress note, hospital day 2. A professional Spanish interpreter joined by video for the entire visit, and all history from the patient was obtained through the interpreter.

The patient is an 85-year-old female admitted with symptomatic hyponatremia. She came in with three days of confusion, nausea, headache, and unsteady gait. Her serum sodium on admission was 119 mEq/L. She received one 100 mL bolus of 3% saline in the emergency department, and her serum sodium rose to 124 mEq/L by this morning. Today she tells us through the interpreter that her headache and nausea are gone, but she still feels a little unsteady when she stands. She denies vomiting, seizures, chest pain, shortness of breath, and diarrhea. There were no events overnight.

Her history includes hypertension and hypothyroidism. Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once daily, started by her primary care physician six weeks ago, was stopped on admission. She continues amlodipine 5 mg once daily and levothyroxine 50 mcg once daily. A fluid restriction of 1 liter per day was started yesterday.

Vital signs this morning: blood pressure 148/82, heart rate 74, temperature 98.2 F, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. She is alert and oriented to person and place but not to time. Mucous membranes are moist, there is no jugular venous distension, the lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema, consistent with euvolemia. Neurologic exam shows no focal deficit and a mildly unsteady gait.

Data: serum sodium 124 mEq/L this morning, up from 119 mEq/L on admission. Serum osmolality 258 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality 420 mOsm/kg. TSH 2.1 mIU/L, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and potassium 3.6 mEq/L. CT of the head showed no acute findings.

My impression is symptomatic hyponatremia, most likely caused by the thiazide diuretic, that is improving after hypertonic saline and fluid restriction. Hydrochlorothiazide will remain discontinued and will be listed as an adverse drug reaction in her chart. We will continue the fluid restriction, check serum sodium levels every six hours today, and limit the rise to no more than eight mEq/L in 24 hours. No further hypertonic saline is needed because her symptoms are improving. Amlodipine continues for blood pressure. Physical therapy will evaluate her gait. The plan was reviewed with the patient and her family through the interpreter, and she may be ready for discharge in one to two days.

Serum sodium rose from 119 to 124 mEq/L after a 3% saline bolus and fluid restriction, and her headache and nausea resolved. She denied vomiting, seizures, chest pain, shortness of breath, and diarrhea, and she appeared euvolemic. The impression was symptomatic hyponatremia most likely caused by hydrochlorothiazide, which was stopped. The plan includes fluid restriction of 1 liter per day, serum sodium checks every six hours with a limited rise, continuing amlodipine and levothyroxine, and physical therapy.

Dictating a hematology and oncology inpatient progress note, hospital day 3. The patient is a 43-year-old female with early-stage breast cancer on adjuvant tamoxifen who was admitted with a left lower extremity deep vein thrombosis. Venous duplex ultrasound on admission showed an occlusive thrombus in the left femoral and popliteal veins. CT angiogram of the chest was negative for pulmonary embolism. She was started on apixaban 10 mg twice daily on admission and has now received three days of treatment. There were no events overnight. She reports that the left leg swelling and calf pain are somewhat better, with pain now 3 out of 10, and she takes acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, hemoptysis, palpitations, and any bleeding, including gum bleeding, nosebleeds, and blood in the stool.

Vital signs, blood pressure 122/74, heart rate 82, respiratory rate 16, temperature 98.6 F, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On exam the left leg is mildly swollen with 1+ pitting edema, the left calf is 2 cm larger than the right, and there is mild tenderness along the medial thigh without erythema. Heart is regular and lungs are clear.

Labs this morning, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, correction, 12.2 g/dL, platelets 248, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL.

My impression is acute left femoral and popliteal deep vein thrombosis, most likely provoked by tamoxifen, improving on apixaban without bleeding. Plan is to continue apixaban 10 mg twice daily through day seven and then decrease to 5 mg twice daily, with a planned treatment duration of at least three months. I am stopping tamoxifen 20 mg once daily, and I will discuss alternative endocrine therapy with her breast oncologist before discharge. Continue acetaminophen as needed and avoid NSAIDs while on anticoagulation. Encourage walking, and a compression stocking may be used for comfort. She received teaching about bleeding precautions. If her pain remains controlled she can be discharged tomorrow with hematology follow-up in two weeks. End of dictation.

Vital signs were normal and labs showed hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 248, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. The impression was a deep vein thrombosis most likely provoked by tamoxifen. Tamoxifen was stopped, apixaban will step down to 5 mg twice daily after day seven for at least three months, and hematology follow-up is planned in two weeks.

note:
Family medicine inpatient progress note, hospital day 2. The patient is a 41-year-old female with type 2 diabetes who was admitted with acute bacterial sinusitis after failing outpatient oral antibiotic treatment. Her sister, who lives with her and acts as her caregiver, was present at the bedside and provided part of the history because the patient is exhausted and has a hoarse voice.

Her sister reports 12 days of facial pain and thick green nasal drainage that seemed to improve after about five days and then worsened, with fevers up to 102 F at home over the past two days and poor oral intake. The patient adds that she has pressure over the left cheek, a frontal headache, nasal congestion, and a cough that is worse at night. She denies vision changes, double vision, eye swelling, neck stiffness, and confusion. She completed five days of amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily as an outpatient without improvement. She has no known drug allergies.

Since admission she was started on ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every six hours. She is also using fluticasone nasal spray, 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, saline nasal irrigation, and acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed. Her home metformin 1000 mg twice daily was held, and she is covered with sliding-scale insulin while she is eating poorly. Overnight her maximum temperature was 100.8 F.

Vital signs this morning: temperature 99.1 F, blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On exam she has tenderness over the left maxillary and frontal sinuses, purulent drainage from the left middle meatus, and erythematous nasal mucosa. There is no periorbital edema, extraocular movements are intact, the neck is supple, and the lungs are clear. WBC is 14.2 and fingerstick glucose is 168 mg/dL. CT of the sinuses shows an air-fluid level in the left maxillary sinus and mucosal thickening of the left ethmoid sinuses without orbital or intracranial extension.

My impression is acute bacterial sinusitis that failed outpatient amoxicillin, without orbital or intracranial complication, in a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus. We will continue ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every six hours today. If she is afebrile and eating tomorrow, we will switch to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg/125 mg twice daily to complete ten days of therapy. Continue fluticasone, saline irrigation, and acetaminophen. Metformin will stay on hold until she is eating normally, with glucose checks before meals. Her sister was updated and understands the plan. Encourage fluids and rest.

She has facial pain, purulent nasal drainage, congestion, and fevers, and she denied vision changes, double vision, eye swelling, neck stiffness, and confusion. WBC was 14.2 and CT of the sinuses showed a left maxillary air-fluid level without orbital or intracranial extension. The impression was acute bacterial sinusitis that failed outpatient amoxicillin. She is on IV ampicillin-sulbactam with metformin held, and may switch to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for ten days of therapy.

note:
Dictating an inpatient urology consultation requested by the cardiology service. The patient is a 46-year-old male on hospital day 3 after a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the left anterior descending artery, correction, to the right coronary artery. The reason for consultation is erectile dysfunction and a question about whether he can resume sildenafil.

He reports about eighteen months of gradually worsening difficulty achieving and maintaining erections, along with fewer morning erections, and his libido remains good. Before this admission he took sildenafil 50 mg as needed with good effect. He denies penile curvature or pain, testicular pain, hematuria, dysuria, urinary hesitancy, and chest pain at this time. He denies depressed mood. He is not on any nitrate and has not needed nitroglycerin since admission. Past medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and prediabetes. He quit smoking five years ago. Current medications are aspirin 81 mg once daily, clopidogrel 75 mg once daily, atorvastatin 80 mg once daily, and metoprolol succinate 50 mg once daily.

Vitals, blood pressure 118/70, heart rate 62, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is comfortable and in no distress. Genitourinary exam shows a normal circumcised phallus without plaques, both testes descended with normal size and consistency, and no masses.

Labs this admission, total testosterone 412 ng/dL, hemoglobin A1c 6.0%, LDL cholesterol 118 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL.

My impression is erectile dysfunction, most likely vasculogenic and related to his atherosclerotic disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and prediabetes, with a normal testosterone level. A beta blocker contribution is possible but unlikely to be a major factor, and his benefit from metoprolol outweighs this concern. Recommendations are to hold sildenafil 50 mg while he is hospitalized and until his cardiologist clears him after discharge. He must never take sildenafil with any nitrate, including sublingual nitroglycerin, and should tell all providers about his sildenafil use. There are no other medication changes from a urology standpoint. Continue risk factor management and cardiac rehabilitation per cardiology. I will see him in the urology clinic in six weeks to reassess and discuss options, including resuming a PDE5 inhibitor if cleared, or alternatives such as a vacuum erection device. Thank you for this consultation. End of dictation.

Total testosterone was 412 ng/dL, hemoglobin A1c 6.0%, and the genitourinary exam was normal. The impression was erectile dysfunction, most likely vasculogenic. Sildenafil is on hold until his cardiologist clears him, with counseling never to combine it with a nitrate and urology follow-up in six weeks.
